title: Carroll eyes new rules amid boom in data centres
full_text:
Data centres would be banned from residential areas, kept away from homes with buffer zones, and be required to supply their own electricity and use non-drinking water under new rules proposed by the state government.
Premier Ben Carroll will today announce new guardrails for the booming data centre market, details of which have been provided to The Age ahead of the announcement, including a new 150-metre buffer zone to residential properties.
Alongside requirements for energy, water and suitable locations, the government will also demand investment in local community benefits.
"In Victoria, we set the rules - data centres must power themselves, protect homes and pay their way," Carroll said. "If we get that right, we can all share in their economic benefits, especially the local community."
The move marks a sharp change of direction from the government. Only six months ago former minister Danny Pearson defended the government's aggressive pursuit of data centre development saying the state was in a "race" and could miss out on billions of dollars in investment.
Since then, some Labor MPs have pushed for a moratorium on data centre projects amid community campaigns in their electorates during an election year.
Under the government's new rules, data centres will be required to power themselves by providing their own renewable energy supply and storage to match the new demand to the network they create.
They will need to meet electricity connection costs and network upgrades. This aligns with the principles most state leaders agreed to at a meeting of national cabinet earlier this month.
Victoria will also require centres use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling, and have to offset the drinking water that they do consume if they cannot match this condition immediately.
Data centres use less than 1 per cent of the state's drinking water but the state aims to keep this figure close to zero through the policy.
In response to the growing number of local campaigns protesting centres in neighbourhoods, data centres will not be permitted in residential zones, with the government committing to ensure they won't be built near schools, childcare or in rural areas that can't support them.
A 150-metre buffer zone would be required between data centre buildings and any home, which the government says is further apart than the standard Melbourne unit of measure, the length of the MCG.
Traffic management plans will also be required to minimise traffic disruptions when the facilities are built and operating.
Under another plank of the government's policy, a local investment guarantee will ask that there be community benefits provided by the developers of data centres when they are built.
These are subject to consultation but could include job commitments or local amenities such as TAFEs or parks.
Centres will be required to train Victorians for jobs, as projects continue to lure away apprentice electricians and other trades from transport and housing projects.
The Carroll government says it will also ensure fair community consultation is mandated and existing noise, fire and safety rules are followed as part of its data centre plan and existing regulations.
Artificial Intelligence Minister Anthony Carbines said companies like Amazon and Microsoft would continue to invest in Victoria even with guardrails in place.
"Data centres power our lives and support banking, healthcare, transport and emergency services," he said.
Campaigns against data centres have become more common as the giant facilities have begun appearing all over Victoria, and the world, as part of massive investment in the infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence.
Alongside local complaints about local such as noise, there is also a broader push to ensure that they are not a drain on communities through the water, energy and workers needed for their operations.
Last month, new forecasts from the Australian Energy Market Operator reported that the number of data centres in development in Australian has doubled since 2025. They were expected to account for 13 per cent of the nation's energy consumption by 2035, up from 3 per cent now.
The Age last week revealed a proposal for a $1.47 billion data centre at the foot of the West Gate Bridge with the potential to draw more power than an entire regional city.
Jemena also halted the rollout of 15 metre power poles in suburban inner-Melbourne streets earlier this month, designed to service data centres, after strong community backlash.
